stimulus:
Soorna is a small brown lake with a deep archive: Virkland's notebooks from the eighteen nineties, the fishermen's association minute-books, and our series since eighty-eight.

The minute-books first: they settle a dating problem. The association paid Virkland's boatman by the day, and the payments are dated, fixing the seasons his notebooks leave vague. Their other contents are thin. The net-fouling complaints are undated grumbles; the argument about the springs names no location, being a quarrel over payment; and the catch was weighed at the landing for two years before the practice lapsed.

Virkland's transparency readings against ours. They scatter too widely to carry a trend - to his credit the notebooks say why, listing wind and cloud for each cast. The scatter is not a steady offset. His figures run deeper on some days and shallower on others, in the bays and on the open water alike, and matching him week for week does not tighten the cloud.

Kivrand argues the darkening began centuries before the first surveys. I reject that. Those proxies move whenever a lake's level shifts, whatever colour the water is - and Soorna's level has shifted. So I am not dating the onset a little later than Kivrand does, I am not pushing it further back on the pollen and charcoal, and I am not calling the darkening periodic either.

Back on the water: the outflow gauge is Tammiste's project; the neighbouring lakes were sampled in ninety-six and written up; the landowners have asked to be kept off the boats. Our first job is Virkland's sunken marker buoys, whose positions carry his depth grid.

options.C: They record the association paying Virkland's boatman, which fixes the survey seasons the notebooks leave vague

stimulus:
Kaldevere's garden, laid out in the seventeen nineties, and the question that comes first: was it Nurmsaar's? The design is his; the hand shows in the sweep of the approach. But I doubt he came. The plans travelled by post, and were adapted on site by whoever held the spade. The estate books enter no payment for a visit; his pupil's planting lists, which Harm compares with the beds, are a poor match; and the family were naming Nurmsaar in their own letters within two years of the digging, not a generation after.

Now the drawings against the ground. Harm reads the showpiece drawing as a tidied presentation piece, symmetrical on paper and loose in the soil, and I would believe that elsewhere. Here the bed edges we dug out in ninety-four sit where the drawing puts them, foot for foot, through the first campaign. Then it was set aside within a decade, as taste turned. The same sheet governs the park and the walled ground alike, and there is no rival drawing to braid it with.

The nursery invoices. Substitutions run right through them: Parnaste sent hardier kinds than the ones ordered. They date the water garden where the guidebooks do; they are made out to the steward; and the estate's own nursery supplied little beyond seed.

Tiidema's letter-book, last. It is a thin thing - a handful of letters, there are no blotting pages bound in, and his famous quarrel is not in it. What it does is show him at Kaldevere from boyhood, against the story that he was fetched from abroad.

options.A: She reads the garden as the family's own project, dressed with the designer's name a generation later

options.C: She upholds the design but doubts he came, arguing the plans traveled by post and were adapted on site
options.D: She reassigns the work to his pupil, whose planting lists elsewhere match Kaldevere's beds closely

stimulus: Crown rot, and how far it travels. We ran spore samplers out from infected stands, and by distance it made no sense. Plots a few hundred metres out caught as much as the far ones. One five-kilometre plot out-caught everything inside it. Deverow predicted a peak at middling range; the middling plots caught least of the lot. Sort that catch by collector height and it lines up: tall masts caught heavily wherever they stood. We measured our hardware. Hedravean. Its harvest books run back a hundred and twenty years, and their bad years let us date outbreaks nobody recorded as disease. Managed ground, yes, but nobody has ever counted its trees — no population to calibrate against. Its growers spray about as often as the foresters. And we went to them: six years in before a grower wrote to us. Moving north? Ferrow says the northern records track our new sites. But those northern stands were surveyed clean twice before, and it is in them now. I credit the spread. Hallick reads the records as movement up the river valleys; the new finds sit north of the valleys' heads. The old southern specimens went back under the microscope — they are the same fungus. Next season, the edges. Our collectors have sat well inside the plots. The spore season shuts down by October, so autumn stays our stopping point. The cartridge readers do more, granted, but want mains power; our plots are an hour's walk from the nearest road. A gauge at each collector would be duplication, not data: rain we already log, from the met station beside plot four.

options.A: The catch showed no steady relation to distance, tracking the height of the collector instead

options.C: The catch falls away within a few hundred metres of an infected stand
options.D: The catch runs heaviest at middling distances, and thinner both close in and far out

stimulus: Trelundy infirmary and its weighing scheme. The dispenser's ledger first: it is a costing book. Extra diet, coals, the man's own hours, priced week by week; the total ran heavy enough that the governors twice set the scheme down for debate, and twice let it stand. Occupancy you get elsewhere: bed numbers come from the matron's returns. There are marginal notes, granted, haggling over the price of oatmeal. We date the break from the governors' minutes; the ledger runs unbroken through those years. The weighing itself. Physicians read the charts as a record of recovery. The ward staff had quite other ends in view: Friday's figures settled who could be put to work on the ward. The scale came in with a physician in the house's first month, and the kitchen inspections start twenty years later. Someone asked whether the balance was swapped — it was the same beam throughout. And the weighing did fix the shape of the week; true, though it is not my point. Maderwyn re-read the registers. Weight and length of stay track each other far more loosely than the reports of the day claimed. Winter and summer intakes gained at much the same rate. The gains scatter across quarter-ounces. The attendants' books disagree constantly rather than running alike. Rostrellick says the weighing shaped admission. His notes come from the eighteen sixties, a generation after the weighing began. Subscribers nominated, certainly, though the house physician struck names off the nomination lists. Until the admission registers are worked through, our papers cannot settle it — and I am withholding judgment on both ends.

options.C: A gap in its pages is the chief evidence for when the scheme was interrupted
options.D: It shows the practice cost enough that the governors debated giving it up more than once

stimulus: Lanmorick priory. The survey of the eighteen forties first. Its measurements read as the restorers' job order: the bays to be underpinned are dimensioned to the inch, the roof they meant to strip is in section, the untouched north aisle gets one overall length. It records the intended works, and little besides. Marrable argues it was a pupils' exercise whose errors march in the order they worked; the surveyors were the contractor's own men, paid by the day out of the works account. Pennoy tells his students the field books beat the drawings made from them; the books hand the draughtsmen the same tidy figures. It did catch the south range that fell in eighteen fifty-one — in two lines and a width. The scan, now. The tower's cross-section comes out an oval, wider by a foot on the river face. It stands plumb to within a finger's breadth. Someone asked about the top stage: it sits true on the axis of the ones below. And the courses run level, rather than wavering as ground movement would leave them. Next, the roof spaces — the first campaign stopped at the wall heads — go up in the spring. Loading was settled last year by the engineers. Repeatability we tested at the outset, on the chapter house. The parish's other early buildings are a different grant and a different decade. The choir's mason's marks. Three-quarters sit in the two rebuilt bays, so they date the repairs rather than parcelling out the building seasons. The quarry marks are a separate alphabet. And the spacing wanders half a foot inside a single bay.

stimulus: The Dunmere wordbook, issued in parts. Lensham reads the prefaces as replies to the reviewers. I part company with her. Beside the subscription lists they are aimed at the people paying: thanks for patience, promises about the next part, apologies for the price. The first preface already names its subscribers, forty of them, before any notice appeared. The passages Lensham matches were in print before the reviews she pairs them with. The staff, meanwhile, got their instructions on printed slips, weekly. The archive is being catalogued. When that is done we shall see how the labour was shared out: each editor marked the material in his own ink, and those marks are on the slips still. Cut entries went with the proofs, and the proofs were pulped. The packets were opened by a clerk who kept the slips and burned the wrappers. The chief editor's annotated rival sits in a private collection in Dunmere. One entry to dwell on: a dialect name for a fishing float. It went to proof, then was pulled and reset — a second pass its neighbours were spared. Its evidence came in from four counties. You will read that its definition survives in six drafts; one draft survives, and a fair copy. Its etymology was wrong, and corrected in the second printing. Last, the slip recount. The collection grew fastest in the very years the annual reports call lean. The boxes for the commonest words are the fattest in the run. For the late letters the published figures run under the true holdings. And the misfiled slips are from the last decade of collecting.

stimulus:
Morgelly's studio ledger — Threlmoor, thirty years of sittings.

Pricing first. Across the square, Ivestead charged one fee for the sitting however many prints went out; Morgelly charged by the print. Ivestead's sitting stood a shilling below Morgelly's, and a group paid that same shilling again. His fee rose twice in twenty years, both times when he took larger premises. One of you had read that he discounted for regulars. His book gives the same figure for a stranger and for a man on his fourth sitting.

Chelvern says the ledger was written up afterwards, for show. I don't accept it. The ink shifts from entry to entry, the way a book kept daily will; the hand is his throughout, which tells us who wrote it, not when. The earliest volume shows the same ink shifts as the later ones. So: not an open question but a settled one — the ink changes at the entry.

Now, the plate makers' price lists. His exposures hold at about the same length right through the change of plates, and his invoices are bound into the back of the same ledger. The interest is not what he bought but what he sold on: the counter trade in plates and chemicals brought him more than the camera work did.

Which leaves the light. The handbook figures reach his pages a good decade after the journals printed them. He opens up a stop for children; past that, the settings answer the sky. It won't date his prints — half the sittings go unnamed — but knowing his habits, it reads as an instrument.

options.A: Its prices climbed each time a new photographic process reached the town, tracking material costs

options.C: It advertised fixed rates yet routinely discounted them for return customers, a practice its own books record
options.D: It charged a flat fee regardless of how many prints were ordered, unlike Morgelly's per-print scale

stimulus:
The measured mile off Aberwynt. In eighteen ninety-four a coal company put a pier across the sight line from the northern beacon, and the course had to be shifted a mile down the coast and surveyed afresh. The navy paid for the beacons and the navy paid to move them. Porthlenny's figures do sit a touch high, but the two grounds were surveyed to one standard and convert cleanly. And the timings came off the ship's own stopwatches, not from the shore huts.

Now, the yard papers, catalogued last winter. What I expect from them is the post survey: how far the marker posts had drifted from the distance the charts gave them. The Penvorran's propellers are in her completion book — the pair she carried into service. Her draught was read off the marks that morning and both sides signed for it. And the sister ship was six months from launching.

Nansveor charges the fleet with inflating trial speeds. I go part way with him. The export figures run high, by a knot and a half, and that was not an error in the current allowance but a decision taken ashore. The home trials come out straight, year after year.

Coal returns, finally. Ships tried in the winter months returned higher figures than those tried in summer. One of you suggested the stokers: sort the returns by stokehold and they scatter less than they do by ship. Trial-day burning sits above what the same ships used on passage. Two yards did return in bushels, and the clerk converted those before the tables were made up.

options.B: To trace how a new civilian pier forced the course to be shifted and surveyed afresh
options.C: To identify the shore observers whose sightings produced the timings the navy released
options.D: To explain why its results and those from the rival ground at Porthlenny resist comparison
